lesson.title: Finishing the Message: How Pre-mRNA Becomes Mature mRNA
lesson.summary: Before a eukaryotic RNA transcript can be translated into protein, it is modified with a protective cap and a poly-A tail, and its noncoding introns are cut out so that only the protein-coding exons remain joined together.
lesson.body:
The RNA molecule that comes directly off of RNA polymerase, as described in the Transcription Overview and RNA Polymerase chapters, is not yet ready to be used. In eukaryotic cells, this initial product is called the pre-mRNA, or primary transcript, and it must go through several rounds of processing before it becomes a mature messenger RNA capable of leaving the nucleus and directing protein synthesis.

The first modification happens near the very beginning of transcription. A specially modified guanine nucleotide is attached to the 5' end of the transcript through an unusual chemical linkage, forming what is called the 5' cap. This cap protects the RNA from being degraded by enzymes that chew up unprotected RNA ends, and it later helps the cell's protein-synthesis machinery recognize and properly bind the mRNA when translation begins.

The second modification happens at the other end of the molecule and is closely tied to the termination process described in the previous chapter. At a specific sequence signal near the end of the gene, the transcript is cleaved, and an enzyme then adds a long stretch of adenine nucleotides, known as the poly-A tail, onto the newly cut 3' end. Like the 5' cap, the poly-A tail helps protect the transcript from degradation, and it also assists in exporting the mature mRNA out of the nucleus and in initiating translation later on.

The third and most structurally dramatic modification is splicing. Most eukaryotic genes are interrupted by stretches of sequence called introns, which do not end up in the final protein-coding message, alternating with stretches called exons, which do. A large complex of RNA and protein called the spliceosome recognizes specific short sequences that mark the boundaries between introns and exons, precisely cuts out each intron, and joins, or ligates, the neighboring exons together. For example, a pre-mRNA arranged as exon 1, intron 1, exon 2, intron 2, exon 3 would, after splicing, become a continuous mature transcript reading exon 1, exon 2, exon 3, with both introns removed entirely. In some genes, the cell can also splice the same pre-mRNA in more than one way, called alternative splicing, combining exons differently to produce more than one distinct mature mRNA, and ultimately more than one protein, from a single gene.

Only after capping, splicing, and polyadenylation are complete is the transcript considered a mature mRNA. It is this finished molecule, carrying a protected 5' cap, a fully spliced coding sequence made only of joined exons, and a protective poly-A tail, that is exported from the nucleus into the cytoplasm, where it becomes available to be translated into protein.
